title: Harlem Lodge Number Four masters and musician members
summary: Caldwell was elected Master in 1949; he lists musician members and later masters such as Eubie Blake, Jonah Jones and Cozy Cole.

story.theme_name: The musicians' union: cards, locals, and the Black-white merger
story.community_name: The musicians' union: cards, scale and the black-white merger

blocks.x: Bob Robinson, tenor saxophone player used to play with fees (unintelligible), Williams and different ones, around New York, and he sponsored me. He was a delegate to the Musicians' Union, Local #802. And Bob was Master, and he
Harlem Lodge

brought a lot of musicians into (unintelligible) Number Four. So he started me off. I worked all around, and he was Master for the lodge for three years. And when I became Master, he was my treasurer, and Lem Johnson, deacon of the blues, he was my junior warden. So when I became master, he was in line, because you had to be senior warden next to master (unintelligible), and that time, oh, we had a lot -- the list of musicians, we had a lot of them on the --
This was at the time you were the master of (unintelligible)?
Yeah, 1950, elected master in December of 1949. That Eubie Blake, Jonah Jones, Buddy Johnson, Cozy Cole, [Jim] Brown, Jerome Brown that played with --
The guitar player?

Yeah. I'd taken them into masonry, Mark We Morris too. All them belonged to Harlem 4, deceased like W. C. Handy and Jimmy Rushing, Big Sid Catlett, Teddy Fields, Lucky Millinder, bunch of them. The musicians you were knowing in jazz at the game masters, like Henry G. Wharton. He came over there to Europe with the Musical Spillers, and he stayed and went to school over there. And he was master in 1945. Robert Robinson was master in 1946-47, '48. (Unintelligible) master in 1950. Then Johnson passed in 1955. Joe Brown, very fine trumpet player. He had an
office down here on Broadway. He was master in 1960.
Joe Brown?

Yeah, Joseph Brown, very nice trumpet man. And Robert Cheek's a good trumpet player. He was master in '61. And one of the old timers, very fine musician was John K. Wyatt. Well, he's playing nothing but flute now. He's a man in his '80's now.
Oh, yeah?
He's a very good lecturer. All these fellows are great lecturers. Then Harry Dow --
The drummer, yeah.

-- he's dean of the study class now. I was dean for the last two years. I got tired, didn't want to be dean no more. Then we had the tenor players, Vernon Moore, very fine pianist. He was in 1970. Harry Reed, the drummer. He worked for the Internal Revenue, worked for the government. He's a good drummer too. Of course, he don't drum much any more. He was master in '72.
Oh, yes.

Then this kid I was telling you about, the tenor player that worked with (unintelligible) me so much, Carl Stretch Ridley? He was master in '73. Then Bill Dow, very fine musician and organist -- he played with Dow when Dow was upstairs in Small's, and I had the group downstairs. He is a master this year.
Well, what proportion of the lodges consists of musicians then?
Oh, this is just -- in fact, this is -- all of these fellows, of course, there's some that was master that passed, that are deceased now.
Well, what it really means if you -- you know, where one musician introduces another.
Right.
Well, the only thing I don't understand, if you're a musician traveling, you know, or in a big band or anything, how do you keep up with the --
Well, a lot of times -- like, for instance, I quit the road, and Lem, he quit the road. Dial, he been working around -- all of us working on --
But I mean a guy like Jonah and Cozy (unintelligible), I mean they're out of town a lot.

Jonah Jones, well, after they get their raising (unintelligible), we'd probably work on a special pension position; after he get his first degree in his first, his mother lodge, he'd get the rest of them in the other lodge where he'd be working. By the time he'd be back in New York and (unintelligible) working, because we only had our meeting on every fourth Monday of every month except July and August, which was vacation time.
